unit.name: The Sociology of Crime and Deviance
unit.subtitle: How crime and deviance are socially constructed, methods of social control, factors behind criminal behaviour, and what crime data does and does not show.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat crime and deviance as the same thing. The spec defines them as overlapping but distinct: a crime is an act that breaks the law; deviance is any behaviour that violates social norms (which may or may not be illegal). Some acts are deviant but not criminal (e.g. queue-jumping); some are criminal but not widely seen as deviant (e.g. minor speeding). Spec section 3.5.1 explicitly requires students to explain 'the social construction of concepts of crime and deviance'.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.5.1 — 'identify, describe and explain various sociological explanations of crime and deviance' and 'explain the social construction of concepts of crime and deviance'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sociological perspectives confused with each other
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mix functionalism with consensus broadly, and Marxism with any conflict view. Each perspective has a precise position: functionalism = society works as an integrated whole, social institutions perform necessary functions; Marxism = society is a class conflict between the bourgeoisie and proletariat; feminism = society is patriarchal and disadvantages women; interactionism = focus on micro-level meanings, labels and interactions. The spec lists these four by name (3.1) and requires students to compare and contrast them on every topic.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.1 — 'different sociological perspectives on social structures, social processes and social issues, including those informed by: feminism, functionalism, interactionism and Marxism'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Studies attributed to the wrong sociologist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mix up the named sociologists. The spec names a specific list and pairs each with a specific concept: Parsons = primary socialisation; Oakley = conventional family; Willmott and Young = symmetrical family; Bowles and Gintis = correspondence principle; Willis = counter school cultures; Becker = labelling; Merton = anomie; Heidensohn = female conformity; Cohen = delinquent subcultures; Carlen = women, crime and poverty; Davis and Moore = functionalist stratification; Townsend = relative deprivation; Murray = underclass; Walby = patriarchy. The Appendix B 'texts and summaries' is the authoritative pairing list.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, Appendix B 'Texts and summaries' (pages 45-54) — names the specific text/work for each named sociologist.

common_misconceptions.topic: Correlation vs causation in achievement data
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'class affects achievement' as a causal claim and stop there. The spec asks them to explain HOW class, gender or ethnicity affect achievement (material deprivation, cultural capital, language codes, teacher labelling, ethnocentric curriculum) — not just that there is a correlation. Naming the mechanism is what earns the marks on a 12-mark Discuss question.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.4.3 — 'identify, describe and explain various factors affecting educational achievement including class, gender and ethnicity'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Official statistics treated as objective truth
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cite police recorded crime figures or divorce statistics as definitive facts. The spec is explicit that official statistics have strengths AND weaknesses and that perspectives differ on their usefulness. The dark figure of crime (3.5.4) is the spec's worked example of why official statistics under-represent crime. Students should always evaluate, not just cite.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, sections 3.5.4 (dark figure of crime, usefulness of crime data) and 3.7 (assess the usefulness of different types of data, qualitative and quantitative data, and official and non-official statistics).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use 'sex' and 'gender' interchangeably. In sociology, sex refers to biological differences and gender refers to socially constructed roles, expectations and behaviours associated with men and women. The spec's key terms list (Appendix A) names both 'sex (gender) discrimination' and 'gender roles' — the discipline distinguishes them.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, Appendix A 'key terms and concepts' — distinguishes 'gender', 'gender roles' and 'sex (gender) discrimination'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mis-allocate examples to Weber's three types of authority. Traditional = legitimacy from custom and inheritance (e.g. monarchy); charismatic = legitimacy from personal qualities (e.g. a magnetic political leader); rational-legal = legitimacy from formal rules and offices (e.g. an elected MP, a judge). Students often call any leader 'charismatic' and mis-tag elected officials as 'traditional'.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.6.5 — 'identify, describe and explain different forms of power and authority including traditional, charismatic, rational-legal, formal and informal sources of power' plus Appendix B Weber summary (page 54).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'poverty' as one concept. The spec needs them to distinguish absolute poverty (lacking the resources for basic survival) from relative poverty (lacking what is normal in a given society). Townsend's relative deprivation (3.6.4) is the key named theorist for relative poverty and includes social participation, not just material need.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.6.4 — 'different interpretations of poverty as a social issue including, the culture of poverty, material deprivation' and Appendix B Townsend summary (page 53).

common_misconceptions.topic: Methods evaluation reduced to a generic list
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students recite generic strengths and weaknesses of methods without applying them to a specific research context. The spec explicitly requires students to 'identify and explain the advantages and disadvantages, strengths and weaknesses of a particular method for a specific area of research'. A 12-mark methods Discuss question expects evaluation IN CONTEXT — e.g. why participant observation is risky for studying gangs specifically, not 'observation is time-consuming' in general.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.7 — 'identify and explain the advantages and disadvantages, strengths and weaknesses of a particular method for a specific area of research'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Ethical issues treated as a checklist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list 'consent, confidentiality, harm' as three boxes to tick rather than reasoning about which apply in a given study and how researchers address them. The spec phrases ethics as 'how the issues can be addressed' (3.7) — meaning students must propose practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefing, withdrawal rights), not just name the principle.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification, section 3.7 — 'Ethical issues are consent, confidentiality and harm to participants and how the issues can be addressed'.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Students leave items blank or guess without reading all four options. With 200 marks across two papers, a single multiple choice mark is non-trivial. Read every distractor — at GCSE Sociology, plausible-sounding wrong answers are deliberately included to catch confusion of the named sociologists or perspectives.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define: Students give an example instead of a definition. A 'Define' question expects a meaning expressed in sociological language — 'patriarchy' is 'a system in which men hold power and women are disadvantaged', not 'when men are in charge of the family'. Each mark usually = one element of the definition.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Identify and Describe: Students identify a feature but fail to describe it. The structure expected by AQA mark schemes is identify (1 mark) plus a developed description (2 marks). Students often give two short sentences when one developed point with sociological vocabulary scores higher.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Describe: Students describe one feature when 4 marks usually requires either two developed points or four discrete features. Linking to a named sociologist or concept lifts the answer into the higher mark band — generic descriptions cap below.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists: Students give a one-sided answer or list points without judgement. The 12-mark Discuss is the most heavily weighted question on each paper and explicitly tests AO3 (analyse and evaluate). Students must: present arguments for the statement (citing perspectives and named studies), present arguments against (other perspectives), and reach a supported judgement. Top-band answers compare and contrast at least two perspectives by name and arrive at a reasoned conclusion.

topic_weighting_notes: Two papers, 100 marks each, 50% of GCSE each. Paper 1 = Families + Education + relevant theory and methods. Paper 2 = Crime and Deviance + Social Stratification + relevant theory and methods. Theory and methods are tested across both papers, not in a separate paper. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 2.2.)

AO weighting is AO1 40%, AO2 40%, AO3 20%. Students often overweight AO1 (recall) at the expense of AO2 (application) and AO3 (analysis and evaluation). The 12-mark Discuss questions are where AO3 is awarded — students should not skip evaluation practice. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 4.2.1.)

Each paper has Section A and Section B, each starting with two multiple choice questions followed by a range of short and extended responses. Plan a balanced revision diet: short factual recall (the named sociologists and key concepts) AND extended evaluative writing. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 2.2.)

Methods knowledge is required ON BOTH PAPERS but in the context of the topic being assessed. A methods question on Paper 1 will be applied to families or education research; a methods question on Paper 2 to crime or stratification research. Drill methods application IN CONTEXT, not as abstract theory. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification sections 2.2, 3.7.)

Named sociologists are non-negotiable. The spec lists 14 named theorists/studies whose KEY IDEAS students must describe. Texts and summaries are gathered in Appendix B. Students are expected to be able to attribute a key idea to the correct sociologist and use them as evidence in extended response. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification Appendix B 'Texts and summaries' pages 45-54.)

Spec content is set in a UK context except where otherwise stated. Students should use UK-relevant examples (Crime Survey for England and Wales, ONS divorce statistics, UK educational policy). Global examples are appropriate only where the spec explicitly invites them — e.g. family forms in a global context (3.3.2). (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 3.1 opening note 'All the content is set in a United Kingdom (UK) context except where otherwise stated'.)
current_spec_changes: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 has been taught from September 2017, with first exams in 2019. The current published version is Version 1.1 (14 October 2021), and the specification has been in steady state since. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification cover page 'Version 1.1 14 October 2021'.)

The qualification is linear — all assessment is at the end of the course in the same series. There is no controlled assessment or coursework component. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 2 and section 4.)

The Appendix A key terms list and Appendix B texts and summaries are the authoritative scope of named vocabulary and named studies. Students will not be examined on terms or studies outside these appendices. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification Appendix A opening note 'Students will not be expected to be familiar with key terms other than those included here'.)
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — disciplinary literacy is critical. Sociology has a dense specialist vocabulary (Appendix A spans roughly 250 terms). Teach a focused 6-8 term glossary at the start of every lesson and require precise use in extended responses. Generic synonyms ('rich people' for bourgeoisie) cost marks at every level of the mark scheme. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report.)

EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (effect size +8 months) — explicitly model how to structure a 12-mark Discuss response: argument for (cite a perspective and a named study), argument against (cite a contrasting perspective and study), supported judgement. Students do not do this automatically. Use shared-write worked examples before independent practice. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning Guidance Report.)

Retrieval practice — the named sociologists and their key ideas are a finite list of about 14 pairings. Short, frequent low-stakes retrieval quizzes (e.g. flashcard drills on study + concept + perspective) outperform single long revision sessions. Each lesson ends with a 5-question knowledge check for this reason. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit; Roediger & Butler retrieval practice meta-analysis summarised by EEF.)

Compare-and-contrast as a teaching frame — every spec topic asks students to 'describe, compare and contrast a variety of sociological perspectives'. Build every lesson around a 4-column perspective grid (functionalist / Marxist / feminist / interactionist or New Right where relevant). Students who internalise the grid have an instant scaffold for any 12-mark question. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification — recurring structural phrase 'describe, compare and contrast a variety of sociological perspectives' across every topic.)

Dual coding — pair every named sociologist with a labelled visual (e.g. Bowles and Gintis = a school-to-workplace flow diagram showing the correspondence principle; Walby = the six structures of patriarchy as a hexagon). Pair the visual with a one-sentence verbal summary. Ask students to reproduce both halves from memory. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit; Sweller cognitive load theory summarised via EEF.)

Sensitive topic handling — sociology covers contested issues (gender roles, ethnic inequality, family diversity, crime). Present each as the legitimate disagreement between named perspectives rather than as a single authorial line. Treat New Right, Marxist and feminist views with equal descriptive seriousness. This protects the impartiality required by the spec's debate-and-evaluate brief and supports the EEF guidance on critical thinking through balanced framing. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 4.1 'critically analyse information and use evidence to make informed arguments'; EEF guidance on disciplinary literacy and reasoning.)

Application as comprehension — many extended response questions are stem-led ('Item A shows that...'). Train students to read the stem TWICE: once for content, once for the perspective hooks the examiner has signalled. Every paragraph in the response should reference the stem at least once. (Source: AQA GCSE Sociology 8192 specification section 3.2 — 'demonstrate knowledge and understanding of key sociological theories by reading and responding to extracts which illustrate the different views of sociologists'.)
